record.paper_title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
record.original_question: For social organizations or collectives modeled as complex adaptive systems, how should robustness, stability, and resilience be distinguished? The question should treat resilience as a systemic, time-dependent capacity to withstand shocks and recover from them, robustness as the structural ability to withstand shocks, and adaptivity as the dynamic ability to overcome shock impacts.

evidence.quote: Resilience denotes the capacity of a system to withstand shocks and its ability to re- cover from them.
Questions • Is there a diﬀerence between robustness, stability, and resilience?

The former relates to the property of a system to withstand shocks, the latter to its ability to overcome their impact. Robustness represents the structural and adaptivity the dynamic dimension of resilience.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a social organization or collective modeled as a complex adaptive system, formalized as a time-dependent dynamical system whose state x(t) evolves under both endogenous interactions among its agents and exogenous shocks. Propose a precise, operational framework that distinguishes the following three notions, so that each can be quantified independently from the others on such a system:

(i) Robustness: the structural capacity of the system to withstand shocks, i.e., a property of the system's configuration (e.g., its interaction topology, redundancy, or buffering capacity) that bounds the immediate deviation of x(t) from a reference state when a shock is applied.

(ii) Stability: the dynamical property describing the system's tendency to return to, or remain near, an equilibrium or reference trajectory in the absence of further perturbations (e.g., in the sense of Lyapunov stability or asymptotic stability of x(t)).

(iii) Resilience: the systemic, time-dependent capacity of the system both to withstand shocks and to recover from them, understood as the composition of a structural component (robustness) and a dynamic component (adaptivity), where adaptivity denotes the system's ability to reorganize its internal structure or parameters in order to overcome the impact of a shock.

Specifically, define rigorous, measurable indicators R_struct(x,t) for robustness, S(x,t) for stability, and Res(x,t) for resilience on this class of models, such that:
- Res depends explicitly on time and on the shock history;
- Res can be decomposed as a function of R_struct (structural dimension) and an adaptivity indicator A(x,t) (dynamic dimension);
- The three indicators are logically independent: there exist model instances exhibiting any prescribed combination of high/low values of R_struct, S, and A.

Show that such a framework exists and is consistent across standard families of complex adaptive system models (e.g., networked agent-based models, coupled ODE systems on graphs), or otherwise identify obstructions to a unified definition.
artifact.status_search_result: The distinction between robustness, stability, and resilience in complex adaptive social systems remains an active conceptual and modeling problem with no universally accepted formalization. Multiple competing definitions exist across ecology, engineering, and social sciences, and recent surveys describe it as an open modeling challenge.

status_evidence.title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses distinctions between resilience, robustness, and adaptivity as open conceptual questions in modeling social systems.
status_evidence.claim: The conceptual disentangling of robustness, stability, and resilience is treated as an open question in current literature.
